# Assumptions

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs` from assumptions/economic.ts and rules/. Do not edit by hand. -->

Status key: **confirmed** = published figure taken directly; **announced** = government announcement for a future date;
**convention** = market practice rather than a rule; **judgement** = our modelling choice (reason given);
**unverified** = a widely quoted figure we could not check against the primary source (shown with a badge in the UI).

## Flagged for follow-up

- **Shares: long-run yearly return after inflation** (5%): Approximately the long-run real return of world equities since 1900 as published by Dimson, Marsh and Staunton. We could not open the 2026 Yearbook from our research environment to confirm the exact figure, so it is flagged. Many forecasters expect less over the next decade; the sensitivity chart shows how much this matters.
- **Shares: volatility (1 standard deviation per year)** (17%): Roughly the long-run annual volatility of world equities in Dimson, Marsh and Staunton’s data. Draws use a fat-tailed distribution: in the model, a fall of more than 25% after inflation happens in roughly 1 year in 40.
- **Bonds: long-run yearly return after inflation** (1.5%): Approximately the long-run real return on world government bonds (Dimson, Marsh and Staunton). Flagged until checked against the Yearbook.
- **Bonds: volatility (1 standard deviation per year)** (8%): Roughly the long-run annual volatility of a global bond index. Flagged until checked against the Yearbook.
- **Volatility and persistence parameters** for inflation and Bank Rate are judgement, pending a formal fit to ONS CPI (series D7G7) and Bank of England Bank Rate history. The calibration needs those datasets, which our research environment could not download.

### Distributions

- Inflation: mean-reverting (AR(1)) surprises around a central path that fades from the 12-month value to the long-run rate.
- Bank Rate: mean-reverting towards long-run inflation plus a real margin; responds to inflation surprises; floored at 0%.
- Shares: log real returns with a Student-t shock (5 degrees of freedom), scaled to the stated volatility.
- Bonds: log real returns with a normal shock.
- Correlations between yearly shocks (inflation, rate, shares, bonds): [[1,0.3,-0.2,-0.3],[0.3,1,-0.1,-0.4],[-0.2,-0.1,1,0.2],[-0.3,-0.4,0.2,1]]. Inflation surprises push rates up and hurt bonds (and, mildly, shares). Rate surprises hurt bonds. Shares and bonds are mildly positively correlated over the long run. Signs are well established; sizes are our judgement.

## Announced changes applied from their effective dates

- **2027-04-06** (confirmed): Cash ISA subscriptions capped at £12,000 a year for people under 65 (the overall ISA allowance stays £20,000). Source: [Cash Individual Savings Account (ISA) limit reduction (policy paper)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/reduction-in-the-cash-individual-savings-account-isa-limit/cash-individual-savings-account-isa-limit-reduction); [The Individual Savings Account (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/1018)](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/1018/contents/made); [ISA reform 2027: anti-circumvention rules factsheet](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fiscal-events-2026-factsheets/isa-reform-2027-anti-circumvention-rules-factsheet).
- **2027-04-06** (announced): Savings income tax rates rise by 2 points to 22% (basic), 42% (higher) and 47% (additional). Source: [Changes to tax rates for property, savings and dividend income](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-tax-rates-for-property-savings-and-dividend-income).
- **2029-04-06** (announced): Salary-sacrificed pension contributions above £2,000 a year become liable to employee and employer National Insurance. Source: [Salary sacrifice reform for pension contributions (effective from 6 April 2029)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/salary-sacrifice-reform-for-pension-contributions-effective-from-6-april-2029/salary-sacrifice-reform-for-pension-contributions); [National Insurance Contributions (Employer Pensions Contributions) Bill](https://bills.parliament.uk/bills/4046).

## Modelling choices

- Both options in a comparison have identical cash outflows each month; only where the money goes differs.
- Overpayers keep the same monthly payment at each remortgage and take a shorter term.
- Overpayments never exceed the yearly allowance, so early repayment charges are never paid; the excess is invested.
- Lower rates for a lower loan-to-value are not modelled (this slightly understates the benefit of overpaying).
- Spare cash is constant in pounds. Results are deflated to today’s money with each simulated future’s inflation.
- Tax rules beyond those announced are held at their last known values.
